pl-l3d1c1-d1e117.summary: Poses the question to be noted carefully: why the Son, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit, became incarnate, since only the Son assumed a man.
claims: Only the Son assumed a man.

pl-l3d1c1-d1e120.summary: Gives the first reason: by a fitting order and a deep counsel of wisdom, God, who made the world in his Wisdom (Ps 103:24), restored heavenly and earthly things through the same Wisdom. The Wisdom of the Father is the woman of the Gospel who lights a lamp and finds the lost tenth coin: lighting the clay of human weakness with the light of divinity, she restored lost man, stamped with the king's name and image.
claims: God restored through Wisdom what he created through Wisdom.

pl-l3d1c1-d1e132.summary: Gives a second reason: the Son rather than the Father was sent because it is more fitting that one who is from another be sent than one who is from no one; the Son is from the Father, the Father from no one.
claims: It is fitting that one who is from another be sent.

pl-l3d1c1-d1e136.summary: Supports the second reason with Augustine, De Trinitate: as the Father begot and the Son was begotten, so fittingly the Father sent and the Son was sent; the Word is sent by the one whose Word he is and from whom he is born. The Father, being from no one, was not sent, lest he be thought to be from another.
claims: As the Father begets, so he sends; the Father is not sent lest he be thought to be from another.

pl-l3d1c1-d1e154.summary: Distinguishes the missions: first the Son, who is from the Father alone, was sent, then the Spirit, who is from Father and Son; but only the Son was sent in flesh. This was done so that the one who was Son of God in divinity would become son of man in humanity, lest one be Son in divinity and another in humanity, or the same be Father and Son if God the Father were born of a man.
claims: Only the Son was sent in flesh.
The incarnation of the Son keeps the same person son in both natures.

pl-l3d1c1-d1e157.summary: Confirms with the Ecclesiastical Dogmas: only the Son took flesh, so that the name of son would not pass to one who was not son by eternal birth. The Son of God became son of man, truly born from God and truly from man, son by nature in both births, not by adoption or appellation; thus not two Christs or two sons but one Son, God and man, existing in two substances, neither confused nor mixed as the Timotheans hold, but united in fellowship.
claims: Christ is son by nature in both births, not by adoption.
Christ is one Son in two unconfused substances.

pl-l3d1c1-d1e166.summary: Closes the chapter: these are the reasons why the Son, and not the Father or Holy Spirit, assumed flesh.

pl-l3d1c1.summary: Asks why the Son alone, not the Father or the Spirit, became incarnate. It was fitting that God, who made the world in his Wisdom, should restore it through the same Wisdom, the woman of the parable who lights a lamp and finds the lost coin. It was also more fitting that he who is from another be sent rather than he who is from none, so the Father, being from no one, is not sent. And the Son alone took flesh so that the one who was Son in divinity would be son in humanity, and the name of son would not pass to another; Christ is thus one son, true God and true man, in two unconfused substances.
claims: It is fitting that God restore through Wisdom what he created through Wisdom.
It is fitting that the one who is from another be sent.
The Son became incarnate so that the same person is son in divinity and in humanity.
